title: Staying cool in a warming Kingdom: Saudi Arabia's cooling-driven energy future

yaml.title: Staying cool in a warming Kingdom: Saudi Arabia's cooling-driven energy future
yaml.description: How rising temperatures and income growth will reshape Saudi electricity demand, household expenditure, and planning priorities through 2100.

markdown.markdown:
One of the less-discussed dimensions of Saudi Arabia's energy transition is that it is simultaneously an adaptation problem. The country faces both a decarbonization trajectory and a temperature trajectory — and the two interact in ways that conventional long-term electricity planning hasn't fully absorbed. A recent study, [*Cooling the Kingdom: Long-term impacts of climate change on electricity demand and household expenditure in Saudi Arabia*](https://www.kapsarc.org/our-offerings/publications/cooling-the-kingdom-long-term-impacts-of-climate-change-on-electricity-demand-and-household-expenditure-in-saudi-arabia/), examines this interaction using the GCAM-KSA integrated assessment model, tracing how rising temperatures and socioeconomic growth will reshape the nation's energy landscape and household budgets through the end of the century.


The most striking projections concern Cooling Degree Days (CDD) — a measure of how much cooling is needed to maintain indoor comfort. Under a high-emissions pathway (RCP 7.0, roughly consistent with continued fossil-fuel expansion and limited mitigation), annual CDD in Saudi Arabia are projected to rise by 40% to 80% by 2100. Heating Degree Days (HDD), conversely, fall toward zero, effectively eliminating the need for space heating across most of the country.

This shift establishes space cooling as the dominant energy service required for indoor comfort. National cooling demand is expected to increase by up to 80% by 2100 compared to current levels. The drivers change over time: population and income growth drive demand in the early century, but the direct impact of climate change becomes the primary driver after 2060, particularly in high-warming scenarios.

| Metric | Projected change by 2100 (RCP 7.0) |
|---|---|
| Cooling Degree Days (annual) | +40% to +80% |
| Heating Degree Days (annual) | Toward zero |
| National cooling demand | Up to +80% vs. current |
| Building electricity consumption (climate impact alone) | Up to +20% |
| Annual household electricity expenditure | +8% to +33% |

## Impact on building electricity and households

The surge in cooling needs translates directly into higher electricity demand. The research suggests that building electricity consumption could increase by as much as 20% due to climate impacts alone — separate from and additional to growth driven by population, income, and electrification of other end uses. This divergence becomes particularly pronounced in the second half of the century as cooling seasons lengthen and intensify.

For the average household, this means a tangible impact on discretionary budgets. Projections show that annual electricity expenditures could rise by 8% to 33%, depending on the specific climate and growth trajectory.

A subtler finding is worth drawing out: under the low-emissions RCP 2.6 pathway — consistent with Saudi Arabia's net-zero target by 2060 — higher household expenditures are primarily linked to improved living standards and greater service access, not to the cost of coping with heat. In other words, aggressive mitigation reshapes *why* households spend more on electricity, not just *whether* they do.

## A call for integrated planning

The findings argue that standard long-term planning practices are inadequate for a climate-constrained future. The study advocates for:

- Integrating climate signals directly into long-term electricity planning and peak-load management, rather than treating them as exogenous shocks.
- Strengthening building efficiency standards and promoting adaptive technologies — passive design, district cooling, higher-efficiency HVAC — to reduce the energy burden before it reaches the grid.
- Targeting policy reforms to ensure that the low-carbon transition remains socially inclusive and affordable, given that cooling access has distributional consequences.

Anticipating these cooling needs now — rather than retrofitting responses after they emerge — aligns with Vision 2030's efficiency objectives and the Kingdom's net-zero commitments.

## What this study covers, and what it doesn't

*A brief note on scope for readers familiar with integrated assessment modeling*: the analysis captures aggregate building electricity demand under temperature change but does not resolve sub-daily peak dynamics, which are increasingly the binding constraint on Saudi grid planning. It also treats the building stock at a relatively aggregated level — disaggregating by building type, vintage, and retrofit potential would sharpen the efficiency policy signal. These are natural next steps for the modeling agenda, not limitations of the current contribution.

---

*This post summarizes findings from ongoing work at KAPSARC. For the underlying methodology and full modeling assumptions, see the [discussion paper](https://www.kapsarc.org/our-offerings/publications/cooling-the-kingdom-long-term-impacts-of-climate-change-on-electricity-demand-and-household-expenditure-in-saudi-arabia/).*
